guides.response_function: Confirms the news happily and expands on B's own adoption
required_content: Confirms B did in fact get the dog
Adds some detail about it — when, which one, how it happened
must_avoid: Deflecting straight back to A's naming problem without owning the reveal
Treating the laugh as needing explanation or as doubt about the photo
guides.example: Picked her up Saturday. I wasn't going to say anything until it was actually final.

guides.response_function: Takes the teasing, owns the predictable choice, stays warm
required_content: Acknowledges the pick is exactly what A would expect of B
Shows no offence — happily stands by the choice anyway
must_avoid: Getting defensive or justifying the breed as if criticised
Ignoring the tease and reporting adoption facts flatly
guides.example: I know, I know. Total cliché. I walked in and saw her and that was it, honestly.

guides.response_function: Acknowledges hijacking A's news, hands the floor back
required_content: Recognises B sat on this while A was talking about their own adoption
Returns attention to A — the photo, the name, or A's dog
must_avoid: Letting B's news take over the conversation entirely
Apologising heavily or treating A's mock complaint as a real grievance
guides.example: Okay, yes, terrible timing on my part. Show me yours again — we can solve your name problem first.

guides.response_function: Owns up cheerfully, playing along with A's fond exasperation
required_content: Admits or embraces that B did the predictable thing they'd been threatening to do
Keeps the warmth — treats A's reaction as affectionate teasing, not real objection
must_avoid: Treating A as upset and apologizing or defending the decision earnestly
Ignoring the teasing and moving straight to logistics or A's shelter dog
guides.example: I know, I know. I held out for about a week. You saw this coming from a mile away.

guides.response_function: Hands the floor back to A's own news
required_content: Acknowledges having cut across A's announcement, or that A's news came first
Actively returns attention to A's dog — the photo, the name, or the update
must_avoid: Continuing to elaborate on B's own dog and holding the floor further
Over-apologizing or making the interruption into a bigger deal than it is
guides.example: Sorry, that completely hijacked you. Show me the photo again—have you got any names in the running?

guides.response_function: Gives A room to absorb it, then names what's next
required_content: Registers that this is a lot landing at once, or that A has more to take in
Offers something concrete about what two dogs actually means — meeting, timing, plans
must_avoid: Playing it as a joke or teasing punchline when A is still processing
Pushing A to be excited or brushing past the fact that it changes things
guides.example: Yeah, it's a lot at once. We should get them in the same room early—before either of them gets too settled.

guides.response_function: Share the relief and confirm the bill is now covered
required_content: Registers the good news as settling the worry that drove the last few turns
Ties it to the electric bill being payable now
must_avoid: Continuing to search or treating the account as possibly still short
Flat acknowledgement that ignores the tension just released
guides.example: Oh thank god. So we're fine for the electric tomorrow — I'll just pay it tonight and stop worrying about it.

guides.response_function: Join the amusement at the early clearing, lightly tease the prediction
required_content: Marks the timing as earlier than either of them expected
Plays off A having called it wrong, without any sting
must_avoid: Treating the wrong guess as a real error worth correcting or defending
Responding only with sober logistics and no shared amusement
guides.example: Later this week, huh? Well, I'm not complaining. It just showed up on my alert too — three days early.

guides.response_function: Wind the scare down and signal both can stop checking
required_content: Accepts the search is over and drops the checking
Names the worry as finished rather than merely paused
must_avoid: Raising new financial worries or auditing how close it came
Prolonging verification by asking A to confirm the amount or date
guides.example: Okay. Okay, I'm closing the app. That was a rough two days for nothing — we're good, let's not think about it tonight.
guides.note: Overlaps with interpretation 1 in tone; differs in that the reply must actively stand down the checking rather than just welcome the news.

guides.response_function: Share the relief and confirm the bill is now covered
required_content: Positive uptake of the news — agreement that this is a good outcome
Practical confirmation that the electric bill can now be paid on time
must_avoid: Treating the sigh as bad news, doubt, or a remaining shortfall
Dwelling on how stressful or badly-handled the near-miss was
guides.example: Oh thank god. Okay, then I'll just pay the electric now while it's sitting there.

guides.response_function: Confirm the good news while acknowledging the near-miss strain
required_content: Acknowledgment that it came down to the wire and that was wearing
Something forward-looking about avoiding a repeat, or plainly registering the money is there
must_avoid: Pure celebration that ignores the exasperation in the sigh
Turning it into blame or a lecture about who let it get this close
guides.example: It really shouldn't be this tight every month. But fine — it's there, I'll get the electric paid tonight.

guides.response_function: Register the news calmly and let the topic close
required_content: Low-key acceptance that the matter is settled — no push for more discussion
Something that takes the remaining task off him, or simply lets it rest
must_avoid: Forcing brightness or celebration onto a drained response
Opening new questions about the account, timing, or next month
guides.example: Okay. Good. I'll handle the electric from here — you don't need to think about it anymore.
guides.note: Differs from 1 mainly in register and closure: 1 shares the lift, 3 lets it go quietly.

guides.response_function: Takes her confession lightly; declines to judge the habit
required_content: Signals the Dr. Pepper habit is no big deal coming from her
Stays warm about her rather than about the coincidence with his water
must_avoid: Advising her to cut down, or praising his own soda avoidance by contrast
Treating the admission as serious and asking earnest questions about her intake
guides.example: Honestly, if that's your worst vice you're doing fine. Whole cooler though — that's commitment.

guides.response_function: Joins the joke about the timing against his water plan
required_content: Names the comic collision between the cooler and what he said upstairs
Plays along rather than restating his resolve seriously
must_avoid: Making the moment about her habit instead of the coincidence
Solemnly reaffirming he'll stick to water, which flattens the joke
guides.example: Day one and the building's already testing me. I said that out loud like ten minutes ago.

guides.response_function: Keeps her resigned admission companionable, not a problem to fix
required_content: Accepts that she isn't planning to quit, without arguing with that
Keeps it easy and low-stakes — companionable rather than consoling
must_avoid: Offering encouragement, fixes, or optimism about her breaking the habit
Sympathising as though defeat were genuinely sad, raising the stakes
guides.example: Some things you just make peace with. I'd never get past that cooler either, so.
guides.note: Overlaps with interpretation 1 in warmth; differs in that here B accepts the habit as permanent rather than merely forgivable.

guides.response_function: Accepts the surrender lightly, without pushing them to quit
required_content: Treats the habit as settled fact rather than a problem to solve
Some good-natured ribbing or sympathy about the habit being locked in
must_avoid: Coaching them to cut down, suggesting substitutes, or offering willpower advice
Treating the sigh as genuine distress needing concern
guides.example: Well, that's that then. One free cooler and the whole thing's decided for you.

guides.response_function: Registers the workplace as the culprit; reconsiders own plan
required_content: Acknowledges the free cooler as what undermines good intentions here
Something about their own water plan facing that same pull
must_avoid: Pinning it purely on A's willpower and ignoring the workplace setup
Claiming smugly to be immune to the cooler
guides.example: Ah, so that's the trap. Give it a week and my water bottle's going to look pretty sad next to that thing.

guides.response_function: Joins the joke and commiserates with a confession
required_content: Plays along with the humour rather than answering it earnestly
Offers solidarity — own comparable weakness or shared doom about the cooler
must_avoid: Responding with earnest concern that flattens the joke
Judging the habit or moralising about soda
guides.example: Honestly, I'd have opened that thing and never left. Ask me about my water bottle again in a month.

guides.response_function: Joins the joke about the hidden-in-plain-sight find
required_content: Shares the amusement at how the filters sat in plain view the whole time
Treats the search as over and the filters as found
must_avoid: Claiming vindication or pointing out that B said so first
Restarting directions or re-explaining where the filters are
guides.example: Right there the whole time, staring at you. Grab a couple while you're down there.

guides.response_function: Waves off the climb-down and moves on lightly
required_content: Makes the miss unremarkable — easy to walk past, no fault involved
Keeps the moment moving rather than dwelling on the earlier claim
must_avoid: Teasing about the confident 'I've looked all along this side' claim
Heavy reassurance that treats a small miss as something needing comfort
guides.example: That bottom shelf swallows everything. I only spotted them because I dropped my list.

guides.response_function: Agrees the shelving is at fault and closes the errand
required_content: Endorses the complaint about the store's layout or low-shelf placement
Confirms these are the right filters so they can move on
must_avoid: Defending the store or implying she simply overlooked them
Only grumbling about the layout without settling that the item is found
guides.example: Whoever stocks this place hides everything at ankle height. Are those the ones you wanted?

guides.response_function: Take the shared joke without rubbing in being right
required_content: Treats her missing them as an easy, ordinary thing to miss
Stays light rather than correcting or re-explaining where they are
must_avoid: Saying I told you so, or restating that they were behind her all along
Turning it serious with reassurance about her attention or eyesight
guides.example: They blend right into that shelf. I only spotted them because I walked past twice.

guides.response_function: Agree the placement is absurd, siding with her
required_content: Endorses that filters belong somewhere more findable than a low shelf
Signals no blame for how she searched
must_avoid: Defending the store or implying she should have checked lower
Making her the joke instead of the shelving
guides.example: Who puts tea filters down by the floor? Nobody's finding those on purpose.

guides.response_function: Close the search out and move on to what's next
required_content: Registers the search is over and nothing more is needed
Points forward — grabbing them, the rest of the list, leaving
must_avoid: Reopening the search with more directions or offers to look
Dwelling on how long it took or who was right
guides.example: Grab a box and we're done. Anything else on the list, or is that it?

guides.response_function: Register the irony and confirm the approval is worthless
required_content: Treats the decision as bad news, not a win, matching A's ironic framing
Names the absurdity that the covered drug is one A already failed on
must_avoid: Congratulating A or treating the posted approval as progress worth celebrating
Jumping straight to logistics without acknowledging the outcome is backwards
guides.example: Of course that's the one they approved. A week of waiting to be told to take the thing that already didn't work.

guides.response_function: Absorb the frustration and turn toward a concrete next move
required_content: Validates that a week of waiting for this result is genuinely infuriating
Offers something actionable — appeal, calling the prescriber, documenting the prior failure
must_avoid: Treating the laugh as amusement and matching it with a joke instead of taking the setback seriously
Minimising with silver linings like at least there's coverage or worth another try
guides.example: A whole week for that? Ugh. Your prescriber can file an appeal with the history — you already have documentation that it failed.

guides.response_function: Share the tired recognition that the system ignored her history
required_content: Acknowledges the futility that A's documented history apparently counted for nothing
Stays alongside A in the resignation rather than arguing her out of it
must_avoid: Immediately problem-solving over the moment A is inviting her to sit in
Reassuring that the system will get it right or that it will work out
guides.example: It's like none of your record exists to them. You've been on this drug already and they just... sent you back to the start.
guides.note: Differs from 2 by staying with A rather than mobilising; differs from 1 by shared weariness over sharp irony.

guides.response_function: Register the bad news and steady her toward next steps
required_content: Recognition that this specific drug being the covered option is a real problem for her
Something concrete to do about it — appeal, call the prescriber, ask for an exception
must_avoid: Treating the approval as good news or urging her to just try it again
Leaving her alone with it — sympathy only, nothing actionable or forward-looking
guides.example: Oh no, not that one. Okay — the prescriber can request an exception; you've got documented history with it. Can you message them today?

guides.response_function: Match the moment, then ask what the decision actually says
required_content: Acknowledgement that the decision has finally landed after the wait
A request for detail about what is on the screen or what it means for her
must_avoid: Assuming the outcome is bad and jumping to appeals before she has said more
Ignoring that something just changed and continuing the earlier discussion
guides.example: Wait, it's up? What does it actually say — is that the only thing they'll cover, or is there a list?
guides.note: Differs from 1 and 3 in staying at the arrival of the news rather than its content.

guides.response_function: Acknowledge the wait ending while taking the outcome seriously
required_content: Relief or acknowledgement that the limbo is over and there is finally an answer
Recognition that the particular drug named is a complication, not a settled resolution
must_avoid: Congratulating her as if approval alone solves it
Framing it as purely bad and erasing that the stall finally broke
guides.example: At least they finally answered. But that one — you came off it for a reason. Is there room to push back now that there's a decision to argue with?

guides.response_function: Joins the amusement and keeps watching for more
required_content: Shares the laugh at the ball hitting the camera
Signals wanting the tape to keep playing or rewound for that bit
must_avoid: Treating the moment as concerning, or worrying about the camera or filmer
Shifting to solemn reflection about the tape instead of enjoying the moment
guides.example: Ha! Right in the lens. Back it up a few seconds, I want to see that again.

guides.response_function: Joins humour by affectionately characterizing his dad
required_content: Fond amusement directed at his dad, treating the throw as typical of him
Adds or confirms something about his dad rather than only about the footage
must_avoid: Making his dad look bad or defending him as if criticized
Keeping it purely about the camera moment with no warmth toward his dad
guides.example: That's Dad exactly — no idea where anything was going. He did that to me constantly.

guides.response_function: Reacts to the surprise and takes up the narration
required_content: Registers the moment as sudden or unexpected on screen
Asks about or comments on what happened next, or who was filming
must_avoid: Reading the laugh as being about his dad's character rather than the surprise
Treating the jolt as genuine alarm about someone being hurt
guides.example: Whoa, out of nowhere. Did whoever was holding it drop the thing? Who even was behind the camera?

guides.response_function: React to the near-miss on screen, look immediately
required_content: Registers the ball coming at the lens as the startling thing just seen
Keeps attention on the tape — rewind, replay, or watch what happens next
must_avoid: Treating A as actually in danger or asking if she got hit
Shifting to who was behind the camera or what it means
guides.example: Whoa—did it hit the lens? Back it up ten seconds, I want to see that again.

guides.response_function: Share the delight, treat the moment as a find
required_content: Enjoys how good or funny the caught moment is
Adds something of her own — memory of Dad's throwing, or wanting to keep/show it
must_avoid: Sombre or reverent framing that drains the fun out of it
Flat acknowledgement that doesn't take up the excitement
guides.example: That is so him. He could never resist. We're saving that bit—Mum has to see it.

guides.response_function: Take up the realization about who held the camera
required_content: Engages with the unseen person filming — who it was, or that it was likely Mum
Gives the moment weight rather than moving straight on
must_avoid: Playing it as a funny clip or joking about the throw
Narrating more on-screen action as if nothing shifted
guides.example: So someone was standing right there. That's Mum holding it, isn't it. Pause it a second.
guides.note: Distinct from 1: 1 stays with the on-screen event, 3 moves to the person off-screen.

guides.response_function: Celebrating the offer with them and confirming it's real
required_content: Explicit pleasure or congratulation at the news
Treats the salary figure as a good outcome worth marking
must_avoid: Undercutting the number as small or a comedown
Cautious hedging that delays reacting to the good news
guides.example: Fifty-eight? That's more than we guessed. You got it — okay, we're doing something tonight.

guides.response_function: Meeting the irony while affirming the offer still counts
required_content: Picks up the wry contrast with the bigger plans once imagined
Signals the job is genuinely worth taking anyway
must_avoid: Solemn reassurance that misses the joke being shared
Agreeing the job is a disappointment or a failure
guides.example: Fifty-eight thousand and not a dollar rounder. Not quite the empire, but rent's covered and you're in.

guides.response_function: Steadying them and helping weigh whether it's good
required_content: Acknowledges the wait is over and the offer is real
Engages with whether the figure works, e.g. against rent and bills
must_avoid: Pushing a verdict before they've had a beat to react
Ignoring the number and only offering vague comfort
guides.example: Okay. It's actually happening. Fifty-eight — that clears rent and bills with room. How's it sitting with you?

guides.response_function: Celebrating the number as far better than expected
required_content: Reacts to the salary as good news, well above the rent-and-bills bar they had assumed
Treats the job as effectively theirs, or asks what the offer says next
must_avoid: Reading the figure as ordinary or merely adequate
Undercutting the moment with caveats about tax, cost of living, or catches
guides.example: Fifty-eight? That's way past rent and bills. That's actual breathing room — what else does it say?

guides.response_function: Pressing for the rest of the email right away
required_content: Registers that something significant has arrived and wants it read out
Asks a concrete question about the offer's contents rather than the amount's size
must_avoid: Celebrating a number A has not yet appraised
Treating the gasp as bad news or asking whether A is all right
guides.example: Wait, so they offered it? Keep going — what does the rest say? Start date, anything?
guides.note: Differs from 1: no evaluation of the figure yet, the reply pulls for information.

guides.response_function: Confirming the figure is real while sharing the delight
required_content: Checks or affirms that the number is genuinely the offered salary, not a typo or range
Conveys pleasure at the amount rather than skepticism about the offer
must_avoid: Casting doubt on the employer's good faith or implying a scam
Only verifying, with no warmth about the news itself
guides.example: Fifty-eight — that's the actual offer, not a band? Read it again. God, that's brilliant.

guides.response_function: Join the laugh, own the detail as story evidence
required_content: Treats the blank tip line as funny confirmation of how gone B was that night
Adds or invites a further detail about what state B was in
must_avoid: Treating the blank line as a serious problem needing correction or an apology
Getting defensive as if accused of cheapness
guides.example: Blank. Yeah, that tracks — I couldn't work out which card was mine, let alone do arithmetic.

guides.response_function: Take the ribbing; own or playfully defend the stiff
required_content: Responds to the implied accusation about the bartender rather than only to the night generally
Either concedes the lapse or mounts a joking defence
must_avoid: Ignoring the accusation and treating it as a neutral observation about the receipt
Genuine guilt-ridden self-reproach that kills the teasing
guides.example: Okay, in my defence, the machine and I were not on speaking terms. I'll go back and square it with her.

guides.response_function: Share the joke while acknowledging the night was rough
required_content: Laughs along rather than treating it as a charge to answer
Acknowledges the state B was in, without being defensive about it
must_avoid: Reading it as an accusation and defending or apologising for the missing tip
Dwelling on how bad the night was in a way that drops the humour
guides.example: God. That's about the level I was operating at. I'm amazed the card went through at all.
guides.note: Differs from 1 in that B leans on how rough it was rather than on it being the punchline.

guides.response_function: Takes the mock accusation and defends or confesses to it
required_content: Engages with the charge of having stiffed the bartender rather than deflecting from it
Offers a defense, a guilty admission, or a plan to make it right
must_avoid: Treating the blank line as alarming evidence about B's state that night
Ignoring the accusation and reading the receipt as neutral information
guides.example: Okay, in my defense, I think I left cash. Probably. I'm going back tomorrow and tipping him double either way.

guides.response_function: Confirms the find and works out what it means
required_content: Acknowledges the blank tip line as the notable detail on the receipt
Adds something about what it might indicate — cash tip, unsigned slip, closed tab
must_avoid: Playing it as an accusation or a joke at B's own expense
Downplaying the detail or moving on to other lines of the receipt
guides.example: Huh, you're right. Nothing on the tip line at all. So either I left cash or I never actually signed the thing.

guides.response_function: Half-jokingly reckons with what the gap says about the night
required_content: Accepts the blank line as evidence about how far gone B was
Tries to reconstruct or admit uncertainty about that part of the night
must_avoid: Treating it purely as a tipping etiquette offense against the bartender
Refusing the implication about B's state with no engagement at all
guides.example: That tracks, honestly. I don't remember signing anything after about eleven. Somebody must have just closed me out.
guides.note: Shares interpretation 2's focus on the blank line, but here B reads it as evidence about their own state rather than a neutral finding.

guides.response_function: Join the joke about the wasted careful timing
required_content: Shares the amusement at the outcome rather than treating it as a setback
Ties the humour to the pointless prep — the held-off meal, the rushed sandwich, the sprint over
must_avoid: Treating the closure as a genuine problem needing fixing or a plan B
Sounding annoyed at A, the gym, or itself for the wasted effort
guides.example: Skipped lunch for this. Ate a sandwich standing up. Ran here. Locked door. Perfect.

guides.response_function: Accept the soft delivery; wave off the letdown
required_content: Signals no hard feelings toward A for being the one with the news
Takes the disappointment lightly — it's a wasted trip, not a big deal
must_avoid: Milking the sympathy or dwelling on how much effort was wasted
Reading A's laugh as mockery and getting defensive about the rushed meal
guides.example: Ha, no it's fine. I'll just go home and be smug about the protein shake. Tomorrow then.

guides.response_function: Match the disbelief; treat the timing as absurd
required_content: Registers surprise or incredulity at the gym closing this early, not just the fact of it
Aims the reaction at the gym's odd hours rather than at A or itself
must_avoid: Reacting with real anger or a complaint aimed at A for the late warning
Accepting the closure flatly as ordinary news with no disbelief at all
guides.example: Wait, already? Who closes a gym at this hour? I'm literally standing here holding my bag.
guides.note: Distinct from 1: the amusement here is at the gym's implausible hours, not at B's own wasted preparation.

guides.response_function: Absorbs the bad news and confirms the wasted plan
required_content: Registers the gym being shut as the confirmed outcome, not something to double-check
Names what the closure costs him — the timing, the skipped workout, the effort now pointless
must_avoid: Treating the closure as uncertain or asking A to reread the notice
Reading A as the source of the problem or owed an apology
guides.example: Well, that's the whole evening's planning down the drain. I ate late for nothing.

guides.response_function: Waves off any fault, keeps blame on the gym
required_content: Makes clear A is not at fault for the late warning
Puts the problem on the closing time or the notice rather than either of them
must_avoid: Accepting or amplifying A's implied responsibility, even lightly or jokingly
Dwelling on how much earlier A could have said something
guides.example: Not on you at all — you couldn't have known they'd shut early. Who closes at this hour anyway?

guides.response_function: Joins A in exasperation at the pointless trip
required_content: Matches A's fed-up stance toward the situation as a shared complaint
Treats the errand as over — a plan to abandon or replace rather than salvage
must_avoid: Responding as neutral fact-receiver with no stance toward the situation
Turning the shared irritation into blame aimed at A
guides.example: Unbelievable. I rushed a sandwich for this. I'm going home and eating properly.

guides.response_function: Share the relief and celebrate the good result with her
required_content: Affirms the grade is genuinely good and worth being happy about
Signals the waiting and worrying is over, matching her release
must_avoid: Treating the number as uncertain or offering to double-check it
Dwelling on how nervous she was or how badly it could have gone
guides.example: Ninety-five! You were sweating that all week for nothing. That's your best one yet.

guides.response_function: Confirm the number and back up that it's real
required_content: Restates or verifies the score as ninety-five out of a hundred
Treats her disbelief as answerable — the portal really says that
must_avoid: Skipping confirmation and moving straight to celebration or teasing
Casting doubt on the number or suggesting it might be a different test
guides.example: Ninety-five, yeah — I'm looking right at it. Chemistry test, top of the page. It's yours.

guides.response_function: Take the light chiding and play up spoiling the reveal
required_content: Acknowledges jumping in when she asked to find it herself
Keeps the news framed as good, not letting the apology sour it
must_avoid: Confirming the score earnestly as if she doubted it
A heavy or defensive apology that makes the moment about B's mistake
guides.example: Okay, okay, I ruined it. But be honest — you'd have wanted me to say something if it was a forty-five.

guides.response_function: Owns spoiling the reveal; apologises without retracting the number
required_content: Acknowledges having read it out after A asked to find it first
Signals the news itself is good, so A can still be pleased
must_avoid: Treating the groan as disappointment in the score and consoling A about 95
Defending the interruption or insisting A should just be grateful
guides.example: Sorry — you said wait and I went straight in. I couldn't help it. It's a really good mark, for what it's worth.

guides.response_function: Pushes back on the near-miss framing; affirms the score
required_content: Treats 95 as a genuinely strong result rather than a shortfall
Engages with A's hope for a perfect mark instead of ignoring it
must_avoid: Apologising for having looked, which misreads what A is reacting to
Agreeing it's a letdown or dwelling on the five lost marks
guides.example: Ninety-five is not a bad grade. I know you wanted the hundred, but that's an A by any measure — take the win.

guides.response_function: Concedes the complaint lightly, then holds onto the good news
required_content: Registers that the delivery or the number fell short of what A wanted
Still lands the point that 95 is a good outcome worth accepting
must_avoid: Only apologising or only cheerleading — this reading needs both notes
Overinterpreting the groan as real distress and turning solicitous
guides.example: Okay, fair — I jumped the gun and it's not the hundred. Still, ninety-five. You'd have taken that last week.
guides.note: Differs from 1 and 2 by combining the concession with the affirmation rather than choosing one.

guides.response_function: Join the disbelief; treat a fourth round as excessive
required_content: Registers that another interview on top of three is more than reasonable
Stays with A's incredulous framing rather than defending the employer
must_avoid: Treating the extra round as normal hiring practice or a good sign
Pivoting straight to logistics like dates, prep, or scheduling advice
guides.example: Another one? What are they even still trying to find out about you at this point.

guides.response_function: Match the wry humour, acknowledge the process dragging on
required_content: Names the open-endedness — no visible finish line to this process
Keeps the tone A chose rather than upgrading it into a grievance
must_avoid: Solemnly validating frustration in a way that kills the joke
Telling A to be patient or that these things simply take time
guides.example: At this rate they'll want a fifth to check how the fourth went. Does anyone there actually make decisions?

guides.response_function: Hold both sides: still in it, and it's wearing
required_content: Marks that being asked back means A hasn't been ruled out
Acknowledges another round is genuinely tiring, not just good news
must_avoid: Celebrating it as unambiguously great news and skipping the fatigue
Reading it as bad news or as the employer stalling on A
guides.example: So you're still in it, at least. Doesn't make a fourth round sound fun though. How are you feeling about going again?

guides.response_function: Sides with the complaint that the process keeps dragging on
required_content: Treats a fourth round as excessive rather than normal or reasonable
Registers that this should have concluded with a decision by now
must_avoid: Reframing the extra round as good news or a sign of strong interest
Jumping to scheduling logistics before acknowledging the complaint
guides.example: Another one? They've had you in three times already — at some point they either want you or they don't.

guides.response_function: Checks how they're holding up; offers something concrete
required_content: Acknowledges the month has been draining, not just this one message
Offers practical relief — help preparing, or a break before dealing with it
must_avoid: Treating it as pure outrage at the employer instead of exhaustion
Pushing them to prepare or respond immediately
guides.example: That's a lot on top of everything else this month. Don't answer tonight — and I'll run questions with you this weekend if it helps.

guides.response_function: Concedes the annoyance, then turns to doing it anyway
required_content: Accepts the interview will happen while granting it's a nuisance
Moves toward the practical — which day, or what they'll need for it
must_avoid: Suggesting they refuse, push back, or walk away from the process
Dwelling on grievance without acknowledging they intend to go
guides.example: Ugh, fair. Still — they don't keep calling back people they're not serious about. What day are they proposing?

guides.response_function: Joins the light dismay and reacts to the requirement itself
required_content: Registers the onstage introduction as an unwelcome surprise rather than good news
Engages with what it means for him — how bad it'll be, or that it's survivable
must_avoid: Treating the laugh as delight or the news as something to congratulate him on
Turning back to whether he should have checked the portal earlier
guides.example: Onstage? In front of the whole school? That's rough. Though it's probably thirty seconds each — name, class, done.

guides.response_function: Accepts the concession lightly without pressing the point
required_content: Acknowledges that this is exactly the kind of thing the portal check was for
Declines to make more of being right — moves him toward what to do now
must_avoid: Lecturing or repeating the told-you-so beyond one light beat
Ignoring the concession entirely and reacting only to the assembly requirement
guides.example: Yeah, that's the sort of thing hiding down there. Anyway — three days. Want to work out what you're actually going to say?

guides.response_function: Reacts with him to the absurdity of the blanket requirement
required_content: Shares or engages his sense that requiring every student onstage is unreasonable
Takes up the practical implausibility — the numbers, the time, how it would even run
must_avoid: Defending the school's policy as sensible or telling him it's no big deal
Shifting focus onto his own nerves rather than the requirement being absurd
guides.example: Every student? There are hundreds of you. That assembly would run all day. Are you sure it doesn't mean per class or something?

guides.response_function: Acknowledges the bad news and engages with what it means
required_content: Recognition that the announced requirement is unwelcome news to A
Some engagement with the requirement itself — its scope, timing, or what it involves
must_avoid: Treating the announcement as good or exciting news, or as something A already knew
Jumping straight to coaching or pep talk without registering that it lands badly
guides.example: Onstage? For every single student? That's going to take all morning. Does it say how long each person gets?

guides.response_function: Steadies him about the ordeal of speaking onstage
required_content: Recognition that the nerve-wracking part is standing up in front of everyone
Something that makes it feel manageable — practice, brevity, shared experience, or company
must_avoid: Dismissing the nerves as silly or insisting it is nothing to worry about
Focusing only on logistics or portal details while ignoring how he feels about it
guides.example: It'll be short, and everyone there is doing the same thing. Want to figure out what you'd say and run through it before Monday?

guides.response_function: Takes the complaint lightly without gloating about being right
required_content: Acknowledgement that his preparation was thorough and this came out of nowhere
Something forward-looking — that there is still time, or what he can do about it now
must_avoid: Rubbing in that A should have checked the portal earlier
Treating it as a serious fear of performing rather than an irritating extra demand
guides.example: Of course there's one more thing. Well, you've still got three days — that's more warning than most people will get.
guides.note: Differs from 1 in that the reply must not scold; the grievance is the surprise, not the stage.

guides.response_function: Acknowledge the bad timing, then weigh whether it's still doable
required_content: Agrees the tonight cutoff is the hard part, not the grant itself
Gives A something concrete about feasibility — how long it takes, what's actually required
must_avoid: Treating the sigh as reluctance about Antarctica or backing off the suggestion
Only sympathising about the deadline without any read on whether it's still possible
guides.example: I know, it's brutal timing. But I looked — it's a short form and a budget page. That's an evening, not a week.

guides.response_function: Take the scramble as decided and help plan tonight
required_content: Treats A as already committed to attempting it rather than still deciding
Proposes a concrete step or division of the work for tonight
must_avoid: Re-arguing whether A should apply, as if the decision were still open
Piling on more tasks or urgency without offering to carry any of it
guides.example: Right, tonight it is. Send me the link and I'll pull the dates and costs together while you write the personal statement.

guides.response_function: Name the upside, then acknowledge the cost of the timing
required_content: Marks that this solves the money problem A has been slowly chipping at
Recognises the catch — it's only available if A moves immediately
must_avoid: Selling it as pure good news with no acknowledgement of the crunch
Dwelling on the deadline so heavily that the funding win disappears
guides.example: Years of saving, and this covers the lot. Rough that it lands with hours to spare — but that's the whole trip, in one go.

guides.response_function: Share her excitement and move toward helping her apply
required_content: Affirms the trip she's been saving for is genuinely within reach now
Offers something concrete toward getting the application done, or asks to start on it
must_avoid: Dampening the news with caveats about odds, eligibility, or how unlikely grants are
Leaving it as pleasant news with no move toward acting on it
guides.example: Right? The whole thing covered. Send me the link and I'll help you fill it in — we've got hours, not weeks.

guides.response_function: Match the urgency and orient toward making the deadline
required_content: Confirms the deadline is real and time is short
Turns to what has to happen now — time remaining, what's needed, or splitting the work
must_avoid: Downplaying the time pressure or suggesting there'll be another round later
Celebrating at length without addressing whether she can actually get it in
guides.example: Tonight, yeah. What time exactly — let's check. If it's midnight you've got seven hours and I can pull the details together.

guides.response_function: Confirm the details she's repeating, then steady her
required_content: Verifies the two facts she said back — full funding, closes tonight
Gives her footing to move: it's real, it's doable, here's where to start
must_avoid: Piling on more information or excitement before she's absorbed what she heard
Treating her repetition as doubt about B or the grant's legitimacy
guides.example: Both true. Full trip, closes tonight. I know it's a lot at once — but it's real, and it's a form, not a miracle.
guides.note: Differs from 2 by confirming the facts first rather than jumping straight to logistics; differs from 1 by steadying rather than amplifying.

guides.response_function: Confirms the mystery is solved and closes the search
required_content: Treats the question of where the cake went as now answered and settled
Acknowledges the cake itself is gone — not retrievable or replaceable today
must_avoid: Proposing further investigation, calling the school, or asking who else might have taken it
Treating the outcome as still uncertain or the cake as recoverable
guides.example: Well, that's that mystery over. No getting it back now — it's probably half eaten already.

guides.response_function: Absorbs the complaint, treats it as typical Maya, defuses blame
required_content: Recognises this as in character for Maya rather than a serious wrong
Signals no further action against her — no confrontation, punishment, or escalation
must_avoid: Framing Maya as deceitful or urging that she be confronted or disciplined
Turning it into a broader grievance about her behaviour or A's parenting
guides.example: Classic Maya. She'd have thought you'd made it for exactly that. Not worth a row over it.

guides.response_function: Sympathises with the lost effort while excusing Maya's intent
required_content: Acknowledges the work A put into the cake and that losing it stings
Grants that Maya meant no harm — she wasn't taking it to be sneaky
must_avoid: Dismissing the effort with 'it's only a cake' or rushing A past the disappointment
Attributing bad intent to Maya, which would undercut the tempering understanding
guides.example: After all that work on it, too. She won't have thought twice — she'd just have been proud to bring it in.

guides.response_function: Confirm the discovery and treat it as needing addressing
required_content: Agreement that Maya took it without asking, treating that as the point
Something concrete about what happens next — reaching her, the fair, talking to her
must_avoid: Laughing it off or framing Maya's choice as harmless or cute
Softening into pure mystery-solved relief with no acknowledgement she overstepped
guides.example: She didn't ask you once. The fair runs till four — want to head over, or wait and have it out with her tonight?

guides.response_function: Match the dismay about the whole cake being gone
required_content: Recognition of the scale — the entire cake, not a slice, and A made it
Some response to the loss itself: sympathy, or what can be salvaged
must_avoid: Minimising the loss or telling A it's only a cake
Redirecting straight to Maya's misconduct without registering what A lost
guides.example: The whole thing? After you were up half the night on it. Maybe there's some left by now — I can drive over and see.

guides.response_function: Close the mystery while keeping the problem open
required_content: The cake is accounted for — no theft, nothing ruined, Maya is fine
It still isn't okay, so something is owed or needs sorting out
must_avoid: Declaring the matter settled and dropping it entirely
Treating it as alarming or unresolved when the photo explains everything
guides.example: Well, at least we know where it went and nobody's run off with it. Doesn't mean she gets away with it, though.

guides.response_function: Confirms the finding and takes the dentist call forward
required_content: Confirms something is actually wrong with the tooth or mouth, so the call is warranted
Moves the call forward concretely — who rings, when, which practice
must_avoid: Re-opening whether a dentist is needed, or hedging that it may be nothing
Treating A's sigh as resistance that needs persuading or arguing against
guides.example: Yeah, there's a chip on the front one. I'll ring them now — they should still be open for another hour.

guides.response_function: Acknowledges the drain and absorbs part of the errand
required_content: Recognises this lands on top of an already hard afternoon for A
Offers to carry some of it — making the call, driving, handling the rest of the evening
must_avoid: Skipping past A's tiredness straight into logistics as if nothing was expressed
Making the weariness the topic — dwelling on how exhausted A must be
guides.example: I know, it's been a day. Let me phone them and take her over — you sit down for ten minutes.

guides.response_function: Names what's found and steadies both about the outcome
required_content: States plainly what the mouth shows, closing off the guessing about her silence
Frames the outlook as manageable — this is fixable, they now know what to deal with
must_avoid: Leaving the finding vague so the uncertainty A just escaped is reintroduced
False cheer that denies there's anything to be concerned about with her teeth
guides.example: That's why she's gone quiet — a tooth's loose at the front. They're good with this at her age. Let's get her seen.

guides.response_function: Treats injury as confirmed; moves to act on it now
required_content: Agreement that the dentist is needed, or a move to make that happen immediately
Some acknowledgement of what A has just seen in Mia's mouth
must_avoid: Questioning whether it is bad enough to bother a dentist about
Downplaying, or suggesting they wait and see how it looks tomorrow
guides.example: Yeah, that's a chipped tooth. I'll ring them now — grab her shoes and the car keys.

guides.response_function: Registers the answer to the earlier question, closes the puzzle
required_content: Recognition that this explains why Mia had gone quiet since the fall
Uptake of the dentist plan as following from that
must_avoid: Asking again what is wrong as though nothing has been established
Reading the gasp as unrelated to Mia's silence
guides.example: That's why she's been so quiet, then. No wonder. Right — dentist. Where's their number?

guides.response_function: Matches A's composure and takes on the practical next step
required_content: Acceptance of the dentist plan without adding alarm in front of Mia
Something steadying — toward Mia, or toward A, or a concrete task taken on
must_avoid: Amplifying the shock or dramatising the injury while Mia is listening
Naming A's reaction or Mia's state as the topic instead of just carrying on
guides.example: Good idea. Mia, you're alright, love — we'll get it looked at. I'll call while you find her coat.
guides.note: Differs from 1 mainly in what B withholds: same practical uptake, but held down for the child's benefit rather than treated as confirmation.

guides.response_function: Match the weight, share the release, confirm it's real
required_content: Reacts to the win itself as huge, meeting the size of the moment
Something grounding — confirming the numbers, or catching breath together
must_avoid: Treating the sigh as a letdown or asking whether something went wrong
Flat or minimal acknowledgement that lets the announcement pass as ordinary
guides.example: Wait — top prize? Say that again. Oh my god. Don't put that ticket down, don't move, let me see the numbers.

guides.response_function: Push for verification, treat the claim as real news
required_content: Wants the result checked or read out again before believing it
Registers this as genuinely happening rather than a mistake or joke
must_avoid: Skipping straight to celebration plans without any check that it's right
Dismissing it as a misread or telling them the checker is probably wrong
guides.example: Read me the numbers off the ticket, one at a time. I'm looking at the site right now. Slowly — I want to hear every digit.

guides.response_function: Acknowledge the win and the weight coming with it
required_content: Registers this as good news rather than downplaying the windfall
Takes seriously that it changes things — something concrete about what happens next
must_avoid: Only celebrating and ignoring the hesitation underneath the announcement
Piling on worry, warnings, or logistics until the good news disappears
guides.example: That's incredible. And also — a lot. Let's not tell anyone tonight, okay? Just us, and we'll figure out the rest tomorrow.

guides.response_function: Match the excitement and celebrate the win with them
required_content: Reacts with shared excitement or delight at the news of winning
Treats the win as real news worth celebrating right now
must_avoid: Flat or muted reaction that treats a top-prize win as unremarkable
Immediately pivoting to logistics, taxes, or cautions instead of reacting
guides.example: Are you serious?! The top prize? Oh my god, say that again — I need to hear it again.

guides.response_function: Press to confirm before accepting the result as real
required_content: Expresses doubt that the screen can be right, wanting to see or hear it again
Proposes a concrete check — re-reading the numbers, the date, the checker itself
must_avoid: Accepting the win outright and celebrating with no verification
Dismissing them as mistaken or scolding them for getting hopes up
guides.example: Wait, read me the numbers off it. And check the draw date — that checker's been flaky all morning. Let me look too.

guides.response_function: Steady them while sharing the enormity of the moment
required_content: Acknowledges this is huge and genuinely landing, not brushing past it
Offers something grounding — sit down, breathe, don't tell anyone, keep the ticket safe
must_avoid: Pure whooping celebration that ignores how shaken they sound
Clinical calm or instruction-giving that drops the shared emotional weight
guides.example: Okay. Okay. Sit down a second. That's — that's everything. Just don't put the ticket down anywhere, I'm coming over.

guides.response_function: Acknowledges the letdown and puts the single lapse in perspective
required_content: Recognition that the theft is a genuine disappointment after A's earlier progress
Something that keeps the setback proportionate — one slip, not the training undone
must_avoid: Treating it as funny, cute, or a good story about the dog
Launching into training advice or next steps instead of registering the letdown
guides.example: Ugh, right when you'd just said he had it. One counter snack doesn't undo three weeks of "leave it" though.

guides.response_function: Sympathises with the long haul and encourages continuing
required_content: Sympathy that the work is taking longer than A hoped
Something supportive about the ongoing effort — that more sessions will get there
must_avoid: Implying A should give up or that Max will not learn it
Skipping the sympathy and moving straight to praise for the dog or the theft itself
guides.example: That's the annoying part — it's weeks more of the same drill. You've clearly got it moving, though. Keep going.

guides.response_function: Lets A off the hook for having claimed the training worked
required_content: Acknowledgement that A's earlier confidence was reasonable given what they'd seen
That the gap between supervised and unsupervised "leave it" is expected, not A's misjudgment
must_avoid: Agreeing that A was wrong to claim progress or pointing out they said it too soon
Piling on about the dog's behaviour without addressing A's own admission
guides.example: You did see him do it, though — with you standing right there. Off-leash and unsupervised is a whole separate thing to teach.

guides.response_function: Register the loss with him and address the immediate moment
required_content: Acknowledges the theft just happened and that it was a setback
Points at something immediate — the snack, getting it back, whether it's safe for the dog
must_avoid: Treating the moment as funny or as a joke to riff on
Lecturing about training method before acknowledging what just happened
guides.example: Ah, he got it. Was that the chocolate one? Grab it off him if you can.

guides.response_function: Push back gently on his self-blame; reframe the setback
required_content: Signals he wasn't wrong to be encouraged — the earlier progress still counts
Frames "leave it" as partly learned rather than failed, e.g. context-dependent
must_avoid: Agreeing he over-claimed or that the training was worthless
Empty cheerleading with no reason attached to it
guides.example: You did say it only holds when you're standing right there. Counter height with nobody watching is a totally different ask.

guides.response_function: Join the rueful complaint about the dog's opportunism
required_content: Treats the theft as characteristic of Max rather than as a real failure
Adds to the shared complaint — a comparable dog moment or a dry read of his motives
must_avoid: Treating it as a serious problem needing reassurance or a fix
Deflating the shared joke by turning to earnest training advice
guides.example: He was never going to leave that. He was just waiting for you to say the word so he could ignore it properly.

guides.response_function: Receive the bad news as a shared letdown
required_content: Registers that the closure is genuinely disappointing for both of them
Confirms or reacts to the fact itself — Marlowe's being closed tomorrow
must_avoid: Treating it as neutral scheduling info that needs no reaction
Rushing straight to alternatives without acknowledging the plan fell through
guides.example: Ugh, seriously? I'd been looking forward to that all week.

guides.response_function: Match the mild annoyance and move to fixing the evening
required_content: Aligns with the closure being an irritating obstacle rather than just sad news
Proposes or asks about another option for tomorrow
must_avoid: Getting defensive about not having booked, or apologising for the delay
Dwelling on the disappointment without offering any way forward
guides.example: Of course they are. Okay — do you want to try that place on Fifth instead?

guides.response_function: Accept it lightly and let the thread close
required_content: Takes the closure in stride without protest or blame
Leaves tomorrow open — another time, or a low-key alternative, no pressure
must_avoid: Escalating into complaint or irritation the speaker deliberately withheld
Pushing hard to salvage the outing when they have let it go
guides.example: Ah well. We can do it another weekend — or just stay in and order something.

guides.response_function: Receive the bad news as a shared disappointment
required_content: Registers that the closure is genuinely a letdown for both of them
Confirms or acknowledges the closure as settled fact, not something to re-check
must_avoid: Jumping straight to logistics without acknowledging the plan just fell through
Treating A's reaction as an overreaction or making light of it
guides.example: Ugh, seriously? That's the one place I actually wanted to go. Damn.

guides.response_function: Acknowledge the hassle and take up re-planning
required_content: Agrees the timing is annoying now that they'd already decided
Moves toward an alternative or asks what they should do instead
must_avoid: Dwelling on the disappointment without moving the plan forward
Leaving the whole decision on A after A just flagged the inconvenience
guides.example: Of course they tell us now. Okay — do you want to try that place on Bell instead, or push it to Sunday?
guides.note: Differs from 1 by carrying the exchange into fixing it rather than sitting with the loss.

guides.response_function: Match the light exasperation, keep the plan alive
required_content: Joins the wry tone about the message arriving right at that moment
Signals the evening is still on, just somewhere else
must_avoid: Treating the closure as a serious blow or apologising as though it were
Playing along so much that whether they're still going out stays unresolved
guides.example: Their timing is incredible. Right, so not Marlowe's — we're still going out though, I'll find somewhere.

guides.response_function: Sharing the disappointment about the missed Blizzard
required_content: Registers the letdown as felt by both of them, not just A
Names the missed Blizzard as what they had both wanted
must_avoid: Brushing it off as unimportant or lecturing A about planning ahead
Immediately pivoting to another dessert plan instead of registering the letdown
guides.example: Oh no. I had that Blizzard picked out in my head and everything.

guides.response_function: Accepting the outcome and letting the plan close
required_content: Agrees nothing can be done tonight given the closing time
Lets the outing end rather than reopening it
must_avoid: Proposing alternatives, other locations, or rushing to fix the evening
Pressing A to check again, knock, or read the notice more carefully
guides.example: Figures. Nine's early. Let's just head home.

guides.response_function: Commiserating about the whole day, not just this
required_content: Connects the closed door to how draining the day has already been
Signals solidarity with A about the day overall
must_avoid: Treating the closed door as the only problem worth acknowledging
Turning it into probing questions about what went wrong in A's day
guides.example: Of course it's closed. That is exactly how today has gone for us.

guides.response_function: Take the news as settled and share the letdown
required_content: Accepts that they've missed it and the Blizzard isn't happening tonight
Matches A's disappointment or offers a concrete alternative for the craving
must_avoid: Asking A to re-check the door or repeat what the notice said
Treating the closure as fine, funny-only, or not worth minding
guides.example: Ah, no. And I'd been picturing it all afternoon. There's that place by the gas station — want to try that instead?

guides.response_function: Join the complaint about the wasted trip and timing
required_content: Agrees the drive out here was for nothing or the timing was rotten luck
Registers annoyance alongside A rather than only sympathising with them
must_avoid: Implying A's slowness, the detour, or the late start caused the miss
Inflating a small annoyance into a long grievance about the place
guides.example: Nine? That's early. We drove all the way over here for a locked door. Of course that's how today ends.

guides.response_function: Play along, commiserating lightly over a small last straw
required_content: Keeps the setback small and shared rather than a real misfortune
Nods to the day having earned them better than this
must_avoid: Heavy sympathy or consolation out of proportion to a missed dessert
Answering flatly with logistics and ignoring the wry, day-capping framing
guides.example: Naturally. Perfect end to a perfect day. Locked out of ice cream — that's the one thing today hadn't taken yet.

guides.response_function: Join the deflation; treat the outcome as a non-event
required_content: Registers that nothing changed — the result lands as anticlimax, not as news
Marks the build-up as having come to nothing, matching A's flatness
must_avoid: Treating an unchanged benchmark rate as surprising, exciting, or significant news
Ignoring the anticlimax and asking eagerly what the announcement means next
guides.example: All that waiting for noon and they just left it where it was.

guides.response_function: Take the news personally; say what it means for the mortgage
required_content: Connects the unchanged rate to B's own pending paperwork or decision
Indicates what B now does — proceed, keep waiting, or accept the status quo
must_avoid: Handling it as abstract economic commentary with no bearing on B's situation
Escalating into distress out of proportion to a rate holding steady
guides.example: So nothing shifts for me either. I'll just sign at the rate they already quoted.

guides.response_function: Accept the wind-down; acknowledge and let the topic close
required_content: Receives the result without opening fresh speculation about rates or the next meeting
Signals the thread is done — moves on, or lets it rest
must_avoid: Pressing A for analysis, forecasts, or when the next announcement lands
Reopening the earlier tangents about cafés, hiring, or B's half-attention
guides.example: Right, that's that. I'll turn the alert off and get back to the paperwork.
guides.note: Differs from interpretation 1: there the reply shares A's deflation about the result; here it closes the conversation itself, whatever the result.

guides.response_function: Register the bad news for the mortgage and respond practically
required_content: Treats the held rate as unwelcome for B's own mortgage situation
Says something about what B does now — wait, proceed, or reconsider the paperwork
must_avoid: Treating the unchanged rate as good, safe, or reassuring news
Ignoring the mortgage stake and responding as if it were abstract economic news
guides.example: Figures. So I'm signing at the same rate I was dreading. Might as well send the paperwork through today then.

guides.response_function: Match the deflation and let the topic wind down
required_content: Marks the announcement as having amounted to nothing
Drops or redirects the subject rather than pursuing the rate further
must_avoid: Digging into rate analysis or asking what the decision means going forward
Treating the non-event as dramatic or consequential
guides.example: All that for a nothing. I'll turn the alert off. Anyway — you said the warehouse is hiring again?

guides.response_function: Join the complaint and commiserate over the wasted wait
required_content: Shares A's exasperation rather than just receiving the information
Acknowledges it was more or less what they both expected
must_avoid: Delivering a neutral or informational reply that leaves A complaining alone
Consoling A from outside, as if only A were put out
guides.example: Of course they did. We both saw that coming, and I still sat here with an alert on for it. Waste of a morning.
guides.note: Differs from 1 by centring shared grievance over the wasted watching rather than B's mortgage decision.

guides.response_function: Enjoys the delight and confirms the gift is theirs
required_content: Confirms the gift is genuinely for them, no hesitation or qualification
Adds something that extends the pleasure — why B chose it, or urging them to open/use it
must_avoid: Deflecting or minimizing the gift's significance, brushing off their excitement
Shifting to the guests arriving or other logistics before the gift moment lands
guides.example: Yes! I saw it and knew immediately. Go on, take it out — I want to see your face.

guides.response_function: Owns breaking the no-presents agreement without apologizing much
required_content: Acknowledges they went past what the two of them agreed
Makes clear they did it deliberately and don't want it argued about
must_avoid: Treating the reaction as pure delight and ignoring the agreement being broken
Getting defensive or apologetic in a way that makes them feel guilty for accepting
guides.example: I know, I know, we said no presents. I decided that rule didn't apply this year. Just open it.

guides.response_function: Lets the emotion land and affirms the thought behind it
required_content: Conveys that B chose this specifically with them in mind
Gives them room to be moved rather than rushing past the moment
must_avoid: Downplaying it as no big deal or nothing, which dismisses the feeling
Making them explain or perform their reaction, or teasing them about it
guides.example: I've been thinking about it since you mentioned it months ago. Take your time — nobody's here yet.
guides.note: Differs from 1 in what it rewards: 1 celebrates the excitement outward, 3 makes quiet room for feeling.

guides.response_function: Playfully owns breaking the rule, presses A to open it
required_content: Cheerful admission that B broke the no-presents pact and isn't sorry
Push for A to keep going and open or accept it anyway
must_avoid: Treating the protest as genuine and apologising or offering to take the gift back
Getting solemn about why the gift matters instead of trading the joke
guides.example: I know, I know, we said no presents. I lied. Open it properly before everyone shows up.

guides.response_function: Takes credit warmly, savours that it landed
required_content: Confirmation that yes, this is for A, chosen deliberately
Pleasure that A reacted this way, inviting A to look closer
must_avoid: Downplaying the gift as nothing so A's reaction has nowhere to go
Reading the groan as objection and defending the decision to give it
guides.example: You've been talking about that thing for a year. Go on—take it out, I want to see your face.

guides.response_function: Reassures A nothing is owed, keeps it easy
required_content: Explicit release from any obligation to reciprocate or even out
Something that keeps the moment low-stakes, e.g. why B just wanted to
must_avoid: Insisting A make a fuss or thank B more, which sharpens the discomfort
Joking that A now owes B something, even lightly
guides.example: Don't start. You don't owe me anything—I saw it and thought of you. That's the whole story.

guides.response_function: Confirm the tally and match the excitement
required_content: Affirms that the gifts really do cover the complete list, nothing left off
Adds to the excitement, e.g. counting items or naming how improbable the completeness is
must_avoid: Treating the completeness as ordinary or already obvious, deflating the moment
Redirecting to the giver's thoughtfulness instead of the striking fact of the full list
guides.example: Every one! Headphones, the books, the sweater — I didn't even think she was listening when I said any of it.

guides.response_function: Join in appreciating Mom's year of quiet attention
required_content: Attributes the outcome to Mom deliberately keeping track all year, not luck or coincidence
Shares the warm feeling about being paid that kind of attention
must_avoid: Staying only on the objects themselves without touching the care behind them
Turning it into praise of the gifts' quality or cost rather than the noticing
guides.example: She must have been writing things down for months. I love that she just quietly kept a list going the whole time.

guides.response_function: Confirm the realization and fill in how it happened
required_content: Confirms that the passing remarks were in fact being noted and remembered
Supplies a detail or example that makes the tracking concrete — when or how things got recorded
must_avoid: Framing it as unsettling surveillance or something to be wary of
Leaving the dawning fact unconfirmed, as if it were only a coincidence
guides.example: Yeah — she had it all written somewhere. You mentioned the headphones once in like March and that was apparently enough.
guides.note: Overlaps with interpretation 1 in confirming the list is complete, but here the reply supplies the mechanism of the noticing rather than raising the celebratory pitch.

guides.response_function: Joins the joke about their mother's uncanny thoroughness
required_content: Treats being tracked all year as funny, with light exaggeration of her note-keeping
Agrees the list was complete, matching A's mock-dismay rather than correcting it
must_avoid: Treating the groan as real complaint about the presents or about their mother
Turning it earnest with gratitude talk or comment on how thoughtful she is
guides.example: She's got a file on both of us at this point. One offhand comment in March and it's under the tree.

guides.response_function: Eases the awkwardness of having received so much
required_content: Signals the scale is fine and no debt is owed for it
Normalizes it, e.g. she enjoyed doing it or the same was done for B
must_avoid: Amplifying the excess or dwelling on how much it must have cost
Playing it purely as a joke and leaving the discomfort unaddressed
guides.example: Don't do that thing where you feel bad about it. She likes doing this — she did the exact same to me with the boots.

guides.response_function: Endorses the affection hiding inside the complaint
required_content: Confirms she really was paying attention across the year
Stays in A's complaining register rather than making the sentiment explicit and heavy
must_avoid: Solemn speech about their mother's love that overshoots A's tone
Reading it as either annoyance at the gifts or embarrassment at their scale
guides.example: Unbelievable, isn't it. You say one thing over dinner in June and she just quietly writes it down.
guides.note: Shares the amused register with interpretation 1, but differs in what the reply must land: here it must confirm she was genuinely listening, not just play the thoroughness for laughs.

guides.response_function: Confirm the find and close out the packing check
required_content: Acknowledges the charger is found and the worry is over
Treats the list check as finished, nothing outstanding
must_avoid: Re-opening doubt about whether the charger or other items are actually packed
Naming A's emotion or commenting on the sound instead of responding
guides.example: Oh good, that's the last thing I was worried about. That's the whole list then — we're done.

guides.response_function: Share the surprise it was there all along
required_content: Registers that the charger turned up somewhere already searched
Notes the recheck paid off, or that it was easy to miss
must_avoid: Blaming A for missing it or claiming credit in a way that stings
Treating the find as routine and skipping the unexpectedness entirely
guides.example: Right there in the pocket the whole time? I looked straight past it too. Good thing we went back through.

guides.response_function: Match the enthusiasm and move toward leaving
required_content: Agrees everything is accounted for
Proposes stopping the check and getting going
must_avoid: Continuing to verify items or suggesting another pass through the list
Flat acknowledgement that ignores A's excitement and the readiness to go
guides.example: That's everything! Okay, zipping the bag — let's get out of here.

guides.response_function: Waves off the false alarm and confirms they're done
required_content: Treats the unnecessary search as no trouble, releasing A from the implied apology
Confirms the packing is settled and nothing further needs checking
must_avoid: Agreeing A was careless, or dwelling on the wasted digging in the side pocket
Continuing to search or asking where the charger turned up
guides.example: Ha, no harm done — side pocket was worth a look anyway. That's everything, then. I'll zip it up.

guides.response_function: Shares the relief and closes out the search
required_content: Registers that the worry is over and the item is accounted for
Moves the pair on to what happens next now that packing is done
must_avoid: Treating the groan as a new problem or reopening the checklist
Reading the sound as a complaint aimed at B and defending the search
guides.example: Oh good, that was the last thing I was worried about. Bag's shut then — what time do we need to leave?

guides.response_function: Commiserates with the tedium and signs off the task
required_content: Agrees the whole checking routine was more fuss than it was worth
States plainly that the job is finished and can be dropped
must_avoid: Defending the list or insisting the thorough check was necessary
Responding as if A were pleased and satisfied rather than fed up with it
guides.example: Every single time with this list. Right, it's all in, I'm done thinking about it.

guides.response_function: Shares the relief and confirms the trip is on
required_content: Registers the news as good and the booking as real
Treats the right week as settled, e.g. the plan is now on
must_avoid: Treating the gasp as alarm or asking whether something went wrong
Casting doubt on the booking or hedging that it may still fall through
guides.example: Oh thank god. So it did go through, and it's the week we wanted. We're actually going.

guides.response_function: Presses for the details now visible on screen
required_content: Asks for or seeks the specifics — dates, times, what else the email says
Acknowledges the uncertainty is over now that it's in writing
must_avoid: Only celebrating without following up on what the email actually shows
Reacting as if B already knows the contents A just discovered
guides.example: Wait, what days exactly? Read me the whole thing — flights, hotel, all of it. Finally something in writing.

guides.response_function: Matches the excitement and helps confirm it's real
required_content: Joins the heightened reaction rather than staying flat
Backs up that it's genuine — double-check the dates or reference, and it holds
must_avoid: Dampening the moment or treating the excitement as overblown
Dismissing the check as unnecessary when A is inviting confirmation
guides.example: No way — read it again? Next week, our dates, real booking reference? Okay, it's happening. I can't believe it.

guides.response_function: Register the wrong dates and turn to fixing the booking
required_content: Recognition that the dates on the confirmation are not the ones A wanted
A concrete next step, such as changing the booking or contacting whoever booked it
must_avoid: Treating the confirmation as good news or congratulating A that it arrived
Reading the groan as being about time pressure rather than incorrect dates
guides.example: Next week? That's not what we asked for. Forward it to me and I'll see if it can be moved.

guides.response_function: Acknowledge the short notice and start reducing the scramble
required_content: Recognition that next week leaves very little time to get ready
Something that eases the crunch — help, a plan, or noting what actually still needs doing
must_avoid: Suggesting the dates are a mistake to be corrected rather than simply soon
Brushing off the timing as no big deal or telling A to relax
guides.example: Next week, seriously? Okay, that's tight but doable — tell me what's left and I'll take half of it.

guides.response_function: Follow the pivot and ask what the dates actually say
required_content: Acknowledgement that the email solved the waiting but produced a worse problem
A prompt for the specific detail — the dates, or what exactly is wrong with them
must_avoid: Still responding as if the arrival of the email settled things
Assuming which problem it is before A has said
guides.example: Oh no — so it did go through, just not how we wanted. What does it actually say?
